questions.stem: Before testing a solid unknown, the sample must be

options.text: Dissolved in deionised water to make an aqueous solution
options.explanation: The test-tube reactions run on aqueous samples, so solids are dissolved first.

options.text: Heated until it melts
options.explanation: Melting is not part of the test preparation.

options.text: Ground into a powder and tested dry
options.explanation: Dry solids do not undergo the ionic tests.

options.text: Mixed with ethanol
options.explanation: Ethanol appears in the hydrolysis practical, not this one.

questions.stem: Which observation confirms ammonium ions in the test tube?

options.text: A brick-red precipitate appears
options.explanation: That belongs to Fehling's solution chemistry.

options.text: Damp red litmus paper held at the tube mouth turns blue on warming
options.explanation: The ammonia released is basic enough to flip the damp red litmus.

options.text: A white precipitate forms immediately
options.explanation: White precipitates belong to chloride and sulfate tests.

options.text: The limewater turns milky
options.explanation: That is the carbonate test's sign.

questions.stem: Why is the test tube warmed gently in a water bath?

options.text: To evaporate the sodium hydroxide
options.explanation: Evaporating the reagent would spoil the test.

options.text: Because ammonia only turns litmus blue when heated
options.explanation: Ammonia's basicity does the colour change; warmth just delivers the gas.

options.text: To drive the ammonia gas out of solution so it reaches the litmus paper
options.explanation: Warmth releases the dissolved ammonia to the tube mouth.

options.text: To speed up the dissolution of the solid sample
options.explanation: The sample is already dissolved by this stage.

questions.stem: The ionic equation for the ammonium test is

options.text: NH4+ plus H+ gives NH3 and water
options.explanation: The reagent supplies hydroxide, not protons.

options.text: 2H+ plus CO3 2- gives CO2 and H2O
options.explanation: That is the carbonate test's ionic equation.

options.text: Ba 2+ plus SO4 2- gives BaSO4
options.explanation: That is the sulfate test's equation.

options.text: NH4+ plus OH- gives NH3 and H2O
options.explanation: The ammonium ion loses a proton to hydroxide, forming ammonia and water.

questions.stem: Which ions are identified by simple test-tube reactions in this practical?

options.text: Ammonium, halide, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and sulfate ions
options.explanation: The menu spans the five ionic species the tests cover.

options.text: Transition metal ions only
options.explanation: Flame tests appear later in the note, but the test-tube menu is the five above.

options.text: Only chloride ions
options.explanation: The menu is far wider than one halide.

options.text: Organic functional groups only
options.explanation: The named tests target inorganic ions.

questions.stem: State the overall equation for the ammonium test with ammonium chloride.
questions.modelAnswer: NH4Cl + NaOH gives NH3 + H2O + NaCl, releasing ammonia gas.

questions.stem: State the litmus condition that the ammonium test requires.
questions.modelAnswer: Damp red litmus paper is held near the tube mouth and turns blue in the ammonia fumes.

questions.stem: Explain why the litmus paper must be damp for the ammonium test to work.
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia must dissolve on the paper to exert its basic effect, and only a damp surface provides the water that converts the gas into the alkaline solution that turns the litmus blue.

questions.stem: A student performs the ammonium test with dry blue litmus and sees nothing. Identify the fault and state the corrected procedure.
questions.modelAnswer: Dry paper cannot dissolve the ammonia, so the test fails; the correction is damp red litmus held at the tube mouth of the gently warmed mixture, which turns blue.

questions.stem: What turns limewater milky in the carbonate test?

options.text: Oxygen from the air dissolving in the limewater
options.explanation: Air exposure is not the reaction's driver.

options.text: Carbon dioxide reacting to form insoluble calcium carbonate
options.explanation: The gas converts dissolved calcium hydroxide into a white suspended solid.

options.text: Hydrogen gas bubbling through
options.explanation: Hydrogen does not react with limewater.

options.text: Dissolved sodium carbonate carried over
options.explanation: The test isolates the gas; the solution stays behind.

questions.stem: The ionic equation for the carbonate test is

options.text: NH4+ plus OH- gives NH3 plus H2O
options.explanation: That is the ammonium equation.

options.text: Ag+ plus Cl- gives AgCl
options.explanation: That is a halide-test equation.

options.text: 2H+ plus CO3 2- gives CO2 plus H2O
options.explanation: Two protons neutralise one carbonate ion to the gas and water.

options.text: H+ plus CO3 2- gives HCO3-
options.explanation: That is the first protonation step, not the test's net outcome.

questions.stem: Why is dilute hydrochloric acid added before barium chloride in the sulfate test?

options.text: To dissolve the barium chloride faster
options.explanation: The barium chloride dissolves readily on its own.

options.text: To turn the solution acidic for colour detection
options.explanation: The test reads a precipitate, not a colour.

options.text: Because barium chloride only works in acid
options.explanation: Barium ions precipitate sulfate regardless; the acid guards against carbonates.

options.text: To remove carbonate ions that would also form a white precipitate and falsely mimic sulfate
options.explanation: The acid eliminates the carbonate interference before the barium reads the sample.

questions.stem: The white precipitate in a positive sulfate test is

options.text: Barium sulfate, BaSO4
options.explanation: Barium ions and sulfate ions combine into the insoluble white solid.

options.text: Barium carbonate
options.explanation: Barium carbonate would indicate the removed carbonate interference, not the sulfate verdict.

options.text: Calcium carbonate
options.explanation: That belongs to the limewater reaction.

options.text: Silver chloride
options.explanation: That belongs to halide testing.

questions.stem: Sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with acid differently from sodium carbonate in that

options.text: It needs no acid to react
options.explanation: The acid drives both reactions.

options.text: One proton reacts per hydrogencarbonate ion, where carbonate needs two
options.explanation: The ionic equations show H+ plus HCO3- against 2H+ plus CO3 2-.

options.text: It releases no carbon dioxide at all
options.explanation: Hydrogencarbonate releases the same carbon dioxide gas.

options.text: It turns limewater blue instead of milky
options.explanation: Limewater's response is the same milkiness.

questions.stem: State the delivery set-up used in the carbonate test.
questions.modelAnswer: A bung with a delivery tube carries the evolved gas into a second tube containing limewater.

questions.stem: Write the ionic equation for the sulfate test.
questions.modelAnswer: Ba 2+ plus SO4 2- gives BaSO4, the white precipitate.

questions.stem: Explain why the carbonate interference in the sulfate test is decisive enough to require the acid-first step.
questions.modelAnswer: Barium carbonate is also a white precipitate, so a sample containing carbonate ions would mimic the sulfate result exactly; the acid-first step destroys the carbonates before barium is introduced, reserving the white precipitate for sulfate alone.

questions.stem: An unknown solution fizzes with acid and its gas turns limewater milky. State the ion identified and write the ionic equation for the fizzing.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbonate ions are present, and the fizzing follows the ionic equation 2H+ plus CO3 2- giving CO2 and H2O.

questions.stem: The wire loop is cleaned by dipping in concentrated acid and heating until no colour shows in order to

options.text: Coat the wire with acid to brighten the flame
options.explanation: The acid cleans; it does not brighten anything.

options.text: Make the wire more conductive
options.explanation: Conductivity plays no role in flame emission.

options.text: Remove any previous sample so only one ion type colours the flame
options.explanation: A clean wire guarantees the observed colour belongs to the unknown alone.

options.text: Sterilise the wire against bacteria
options.explanation: Sterility is irrelevant to the emission test.

questions.stem: Why does a wire glowing red-hot confuse the flame colour reading?

options.text: The wire would melt at that temperature
options.explanation: Nichrome survives far beyond a red glow.

options.text: The sample would evaporate completely
options.explanation: Some volatilisation is normal; the confusion concern is the glow.

options.text: Red light indicates a failed test
options.explanation: The concern is misleading colour, not pass-fail signalling.

options.text: The red glow of hot wire can be confused with a genuine flame colour
options.explanation: Self-emission from hot metal would masquerade as the sample's colour.

questions.stem: Flame tests identify metal ions because

options.text: Each metal ion emits its own characteristic colour when heated strongly
options.explanation: The element's electronic structure sets its emission fingerprint.

options.text: Every metal burns with the same colour
options.explanation: Distinct colours are the method's entire basis.

options.text: The acid changes colour with each metal
options.explanation: The acid is the cleaner, not the indicator.

options.text: The Bunsen flame itself changes with the metal
options.explanation: The flame's blue cone stays; the colour comes from the ion.

questions.stem: Two metal ions heated on the same wire produce what flame outcome?

options.text: The colour of whichever ion is heavier
options.explanation: Emission depends on electronic structure, not mass.

options.text: Mixed colours that make identification erroneous
options.explanation: Superimposed emissions blur the signature the method relies on.

options.text: A new, third colour unique to the mixture
options.explanation: The emissions add, they do not chemically react into a new colour.

options.text: No colour at all
options.explanation: Both ions still emit; the result is a jumble, not silence.

questions.stem: Where in the flame should the loaded wire be held?

options.text: Above the flame entirely, in the air
options.explanation: Above the flame the sample receives no heat.

options.text: Touching the burner barrel
options.explanation: That heats the wire without sampling properly.

options.text: At the edge of the blue Bunsen flame
options.explanation: The edge gives the strong, readable emission zone.

options.text: Deep inside the blue cone
options.explanation: The hot cone is for cleaning, not sampling.

questions.stem: State the two wire materials used for flame tests.
questions.modelAnswer: Unreactive metal wires such as nichrome or platinum are used for the loop.

questions.stem: State the precondition that makes a flame colour readable.
questions.modelAnswer: The test works only when a single type of ion is present, which is why the wire is cleaned until it shows no colour.

questions.stem: Explain why the flame test cannot reliably identify a mixture of two metal ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Each ion emits its own colour simultaneously, and the superimposed emissions blend in the flame, so the observed colour no longer matches either ion's clean signature and the identification becomes erroneous.

questions.stem: A wire shows a persistent yellow flame even after one acid dip. Suggest the fault and the corrective action before running the unknown test.
questions.modelAnswer: Residual contamination, most commonly sodium, still colours the flame; the corrective action is repeating the acid-dip-and-burn cycle until the flame shows no colour at all, then loading the unknown.
